1.summary: As David lies old and frail, his son Adonijah claims the throne; Nathan and Bathsheba remind David of his promise, and David has Solomon anointed king at the Gihon spring.
1.lookfor: Notice who supports each son, how Nathan and Bathsheba work together, and how quickly Adonijah's party scatters.

names.name: Abishag
names.gloss: A young woman from Shunem brought to care for the aged David.

names.name: Adonijah
names.gloss: David's fourth son, the eldest surviving, who claims the throne.

names.name: Joab
names.gloss: David's long-serving army commander, who backs Adonijah.

names.name: Abiathar
names.gloss: A priest who served David since his outlaw days, also backing Adonijah.

names.name: Zadok
names.gloss: A priest loyal to David and Solomon.

names.name: Nathan
names.gloss: The prophet who had promised David a dynasty and rebuked him over Bathsheba.

names.name: Benaiah
names.gloss: Commander of David's bodyguard.

names.name: Gihon
names.gloss: The main spring of Jerusalem, just outside the old city.

insights.title: Couldn't keep warm
insights.body: The book opens with the great king unable to keep warm (1:1). Abishag is brought to care for him, but "the king didn't know her" (1:4). The scene shows David's weakness and sets up a later conflict over Abishag.

insights.title: Never disciplined
insights.body: Adonijah announces "I will be king" with chariots and runners, like Absalom before him (1:5). The narrator adds that David "had not displeased him at any time" by asking why he acted as he did (1:6). David's failure as a father appears again.

insights.title: Two parties
insights.body: Joab and Abiathar back Adonijah; Zadok, Benaiah, Nathan and David's mighty men do not (1:7-8). The old guard of David's outlaw years splits. Solomon's reign begins with factions that he will deal with ruthlessly in chapter 2.

insights.title: Nathan and Bathsheba
insights.body: Nathan coaches Bathsheba to remind David of an oath that Solomon would reign (1:13), then comes in to confirm her words (1:22-27). Readers debate whether the oath was real, since the earlier books never record it; the text presents David as remembering it.

insights.title: Riding the king's mule
insights.body: David orders Solomon to ride his own mule down to the Gihon, to be anointed by Zadok and Nathan with trumpets and shouts of "Long live king Solomon!" (1:33-34). Riding the king's animal was a public sign of succession. Jesus' entry into Jerusalem on a donkey drew on royal imagery like this.

insights.title: The earth split
insights.body: The crowd rejoices so loudly "that the earth shook with their sound" (1:40). Adonijah's guests hear it at their feast, and when the news comes they scatter (1:49). Adonijah runs to the altar and grabs its horns for sanctuary (1:50).

insights.title: Passing the baton
insights.body: David's failure to settle his succession nearly caused a civil war. What do you need to settle now so that others are not left in confusion later?

2.summary: David charges Solomon to keep God's law and to deal with Joab and Shimei, then dies; Solomon secures his throne by executing Adonijah, Joab and Shimei and banishing Abiathar.
2.lookfor: Notice David's two kinds of instruction, Adonijah's request, and how each enemy is dealt with.

names.name: Shimei
names.gloss: The Benjamite who cursed David during Absalom's revolt.

names.name: Barzillai
names.gloss: The Gileadite who fed David's men in exile.

names.name: Anathoth
names.gloss: A priestly town in Benjamin, later Jeremiah's home.

names.name: Kidron
names.gloss: The brook east of Jerusalem that Shimei must not cross.

insights.title: Show yourself a man
insights.body: David's last words begin, "I am going the way of all the earth. You be strong therefore, and show yourself a man" (2:2), echoing Joshua's farewell. He tells Solomon to keep the law of Moses so that God's promise of a lasting throne will stand (2:3-4).

insights.title: Unfinished business
insights.body: David tells Solomon not to let Joab's "gray head go down to Sheol in peace" for the murders of Abner and Amasa (2:5-6), and to deal with Shimei (2:9). Readers are divided: some see justice long delayed, others a dying king settling scores. The text records it without comment.

insights.title: Asking for Abishag
insights.body: Adonijah asks Bathsheba to request Abishag as his wife (2:17). Taking a former king's woman signalled a claim to his throne, as Absalom showed. Solomon sees the danger at once and has him executed (2:22-25).

insights.title: Abiathar banished
insights.body: Solomon sends Abiathar home to Anathoth, "that he might fulfill Yahweh's word which he spoke concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh" (2:27). The prophecy against Eli's family is completed generations later.

insights.title: Holding the altar
insights.body: Joab flees to the altar and holds its horns (2:28), but Benaiah kills him there (2:34). The Law allowed a deliberate murderer to be taken even from God's altar.

insights.title: Shimei's line
insights.body: Shimei agrees to stay in Jerusalem and never cross the Kidron (2:36-38). Three years later he leaves to chase runaway slaves and is executed (2:39-46). He breaks his own oath.

insights.title: Established in his hand
insights.body: "The kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon" (2:46). It is secured by bloodshed rather than by peace. Solomon's reign begins with the same mix of faith and political violence that marked David's.

insights.title: Mercy and judgment
insights.body: David spared Shimei but asked Solomon to punish him later. How do you hold together forgiveness and justice?

3.summary: Solomon marries Pharaoh's daughter and worships at the high places; at Gibeon God offers him anything, and he asks for wisdom to govern, which he soon shows by judging between two mothers claiming one baby.
3.lookfor: Notice the mixed note at the start, what Solomon asks for and why, and how the case of the two women is solved.

names.name: Pharaoh
names.gloss: The king of Egypt, whose daughter Solomon married.

names.name: Gibeon
names.gloss: A town north of Jerusalem with the most important high place, where the tabernacle stood.

insights.title: Pharaoh's daughter
insights.body: Solomon makes an alliance with Egypt by marrying Pharaoh's daughter (3:1). For Israel's king to marry an Egyptian princess shows his prestige; Egyptian pharaohs rarely gave daughters to foreign kings. It also hints at the foreign marriages that will turn his heart.

insights.title: The high places
insights.body: "The people sacrificed in the high places" because there was no Temple yet (3:2), and Solomon himself offered a thousand burnt offerings at Gibeon (3:4). High places were hilltop shrines. Kings later is critical of them once the Temple exists.

insights.title: Ask what I shall give you
insights.body: God appears in a dream: "Ask for what I should give you" (3:5). Solomon calls himself "a little child" who doesn't know how to go out or come in (3:7). Humility comes before wisdom.

insights.title: A hearing heart
insights.body: Solomon asks for "an understanding heart to judge your people" (3:9). The Hebrew is literally "a hearing heart," lev shomea. Wisdom begins with listening, to God and to people.

insights.title: What he didn't ask
insights.body: God is pleased that Solomon did not ask for long life, riches or his enemies' lives (3:11), and gives him those as well (3:13). Jesus' teaching to seek God's kingdom first and the rest will be added echoes this.

insights.title: Two mothers, one child
insights.body: Two prostitutes claim the same baby. Solomon orders it cut in two; the real mother would rather give it up than see it die (3:26). The famous judgment shows "the wisdom of God was in him" (3:28).

insights.title: Wisdom for justice
insights.body: Solomon's gift is not wisdom in general but wisdom "to discern justice" (3:11). The first case shows it serving two of the lowest people in society. Psalm 72, linked to Solomon, prays for a king who defends the poor.

insights.title: Your request
insights.body: If God asked what to give you, what would you ask for, and what would your answer show about your heart? Solomon asked for a listening heart to serve others well, and God added what he did not ask for.

4.summary: A list of Solomon's officials and twelve district governors, the daily provisions for his court, and praise of his peace, prosperity and great wisdom.
4.lookfor: Notice the districts that supply the court, the picture of peace, and the description of Solomon's wisdom.

names.name: Azariah
names.gloss: Son of Zadok, one of Solomon's chief officials.

names.name: Adoniram
names.gloss: Officer over forced labour.

names.name: Ethan the Ezrahite
names.gloss: A famous wise man; Psalm 89 is credited to him.

skim.advice: Verses 1 to 19 list Solomon's officials and the twelve districts. Skim the names and read verses 20 to 34 closely.

insights.title: Twelve districts
insights.body: Solomon divides the land into twelve districts, each supplying the court for one month (4:7). The districts do not match the tribal borders exactly, and Judah seems to be left out. Many scholars think this administration, and the heavy demands it made, fed the north's later resentment.

insights.title: One day's food
insights.body: The court's daily provisions include thirty cors of fine flour, sixty of meal, thirty cattle and a hundred sheep, besides deer and fowl (4:22-23). Samuel had warned that a king would take the people's produce.

insights.title: Like the sand of the sea
insights.body: "Judah and Israel were numerous as the sand which is by the sea in multitude, eating and drinking and making merry" (4:20). God's promise to Abraham of descendants like the sand seems fulfilled in Solomon's day.

insights.title: Under vine and fig tree
insights.body: "Every man under his vine and under his fig tree" (4:25) became a classic image of peace and security. Micah uses it for the coming age of peace, and Zechariah too.

insights.title: Wiser than the East
insights.body: Solomon's wisdom "excelled the wisdom of all the children of the east, and all the wisdom of Egypt" (4:30). Wisdom literature was an international tradition; Egyptian instruction texts like that of Amenemope have close parallels in Proverbs.

insights.title: Proverbs and songs
insights.body: "He spoke three thousand proverbs; and his songs numbered one thousand five" (4:32). He spoke about trees, animals, birds and fish (4:33). Proverbs, the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes are traditionally linked to him.

insights.title: Wisdom about creation
insights.body: Solomon's wisdom included plants and animals. How might studying God's creation be part of growing wise?

5.summary: Solomon makes a treaty with Hiram king of Tyre for cedar and cypress from Lebanon, and drafts tens of thousands of Israelites into forced labour to prepare materials for the Temple.
5.lookfor: Notice why Solomon can build when David could not, what each king supplies, and the scale of the labour force.

names.name: Hiram
names.gloss: King of Tyre, the Phoenician port, a friend of David.

names.name: Lebanon
names.gloss: The mountains north of Israel, famous for cedar forests.

names.name: Gebalites
names.gloss: Craftsmen from Gebal, the Phoenician city later called Byblos.

insights.title: Rest on every side
insights.body: Solomon tells Hiram that David could not build because of constant war, "But now Yahweh my God has given me rest on every side" (5:4). God had promised that David's son would build the house.

insights.title: Cedars of Lebanon
insights.body: Lebanon's cedars were prized across the ancient world for temples and palaces; Mesopotamian and Egyptian kings boasted of obtaining them. The logs were floated as rafts down the coast (5:9). Only scattered groves survive today.

insights.title: Wheat and oil for timber
insights.body: In return for timber, Solomon sends Hiram wheat and pure oil every year (5:11). Phoenicia had timber but little farmland; Israel had grain and olives. The trade suits both.

insights.title: Forced labour
insights.body: Solomon drafts thirty thousand men from all Israel, working in Lebanon one month in three (5:13-14), plus seventy thousand carriers and eighty thousand stonecutters (5:15). Samuel's warning about the king taking sons for his work is being fulfilled.

insights.title: Hiram blesses Yahweh
insights.body: The Phoenician king says, "Blessed is Yahweh today, who has given to David a wise son" (5:7). Foreigners recognise Israel's God through Solomon's wisdom, a theme that returns with the queen of Sheba.

insights.title: Peace with Hiram
insights.body: "There was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a treaty together" (5:12). Solomon's name comes from shalom, peace. His reign is marked by alliances rather than conquests.

insights.title: The cost of building
insights.body: The Temple was built with great faith and great human cost. How do you weigh the cost to people in what you build for God?

6.summary: Solomon builds the Temple over seven years: its stone structure, cedar panelling overlaid with gold, the inner sanctuary with two great cherubim, and carvings of palm trees and flowers.
6.lookfor: Notice the date given at the start, the silence of the building site, God's word in the middle, and the decoration.

names.name: cherubim
names.gloss: Winged heavenly guardians, carved in olive wood and covered in gold.

skim.advice: Much of the chapter gives measurements and building details. Skim them, and read verses 1, 7, 11 to 13 and 23 to 28 closely.

insights.title: The 480th year
insights.body: The Temple was begun "in the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Israel had come out of the land of Egypt" (6:1). On a literal reading this dates the exodus to around 1446 BC. Others see 480 as twelve generations of forty years, a symbolic figure.

insights.title: A temple plan
insights.body: The Temple had a porch, a main hall and an inner sanctuary (6:2-3, 6:16), about thirty metres long. Temples with this three-part plan have been found in Syria, such as at Ain Dara. Israel's Temple used a familiar design for a unique God.

insights.title: No hammer heard
insights.body: "No hammer or ax or any tool of iron was heard in the house while it was under construction" (6:7). The stones were finished at the quarry. Jewish tradition connected this with the Law's ban on iron tools for the altar.

insights.title: The word in the middle
insights.body: In the middle of the building account God speaks: "if you will walk in my statutes... I will dwell among the children of Israel" (6:12-13). The building does not guarantee God's presence; obedience does.

insights.title: Cherubim of olive wood
insights.body: Two cherubim of olive wood, overlaid with gold, ten cubits high, stand in the inner sanctuary with wings touching wall to wall (6:23-27). Winged guardian figures flanked thrones and sacred spaces across the ancient Near East.

insights.title: Garden imagery
insights.body: The walls are carved with cherubim, palm trees and open flowers (6:29). Many scholars see the Temple as a picture of Eden, the garden where God walked with humanity, guarded by cherubim. Revelation ends with a city that is also a garden.

insights.title: Seven years
insights.body: The Temple took seven years to build (6:38); Solomon's own palace took thirteen (7:1). Some readers see a quiet comment on Solomon's priorities.

insights.title: Silent building
insights.body: The Temple went up without the sound of iron tools. What quiet work is God doing in you that no one can hear?

7.summary: Solomon builds his palace and public halls over thirteen years, and Hiram the bronze worker casts the Temple's great bronze pillars, the bronze sea, stands and basins.
7.lookfor: Notice how long the palace took, the names of the two pillars, and the size of the bronze sea.

names.name: Forest of Lebanon
names.gloss: A great hall of Solomon's palace, named for its many cedar pillars.

skim.advice: Most of the chapter describes buildings and bronze work in detail. Skim the measurements, and read about the palace (verses 1 to 12), the pillars (15 to 22) and the sea (23 to 26).

insights.title: Thirteen years
insights.body: "Solomon was building his own house thirteen years" (7:1), nearly twice the Temple's seven. The narrator places the palace account inside the Temple account, perhaps to invite comparison.

insights.title: House of the Forest of Lebanon
insights.body: The great hall had forty-five cedar pillars in rows (7:2-3), like a forest. It later stored gold shields (10:17). Royal complexes in the region had similar pillared halls.

insights.title: Hiram the craftsman
insights.body: A different Hiram, a bronze worker from Tyre, makes the Temple bronzes. His mother was a widow of Naphtali (7:14). Like Bezalel for the tabernacle, he is "filled with wisdom and understanding" (7:14).

insights.title: Jachin and Boaz
insights.body: The two bronze pillars at the porch are named Jachin, probably meaning he will establish, and Boaz, probably meaning in him is strength (7:21). Their exact meaning is uncertain; they may have been the opening words of royal inscriptions.

insights.title: The bronze sea
insights.body: The "molten sea" was a huge round basin of cast bronze about five metres across, standing on twelve bronze oxen facing outward (7:23-25). Chronicles says it was for the priests to wash in. In the ancient world the sea often symbolised chaos; here it is tamed and set in God's house.

insights.title: Pi as three
insights.body: The sea is ten cubits across and thirty cubits round (7:23), which works out pi as three. Explanations include rounded numbers, measuring the inside diameter and outside circumference, or the flared lip described in verse 26.

insights.title: Carried to Babylon
insights.body: The pillars, stands and sea are broken up and carried to Babylon when Jerusalem falls (2 Kings 25:13). Kings records their loss in detail, as if mourning them.

insights.title: Skill for God
insights.body: Hiram's craftsmanship served God's house. How can your skills be offered to God?

8.summary: The ark is brought into the Temple, the cloud of God's glory fills it, and Solomon blesses the people, prays a long prayer of dedication, and holds a fourteen-day feast.
8.lookfor: Notice what was in the ark, the cloud, the question Solomon asks about God's dwelling, and the repeated request "hear in heaven."

names.name: Horeb
names.gloss: Mount Sinai, where the covenant was given.

insights.title: Only the tablets
insights.body: "There was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets" (8:9). Hebrews mentions a pot of manna and Aaron's rod as well; by Solomon's time, Kings says, only the tablets remained. The heart of the Temple is God's covenant word.

insights.title: The cloud fills the house
insights.body: "The cloud filled Yahweh's house, so that the priests could not stand to minister" (8:10-11). The same happened when the tabernacle was finished. God accepts the house as his dwelling.

insights.title: Can heaven contain you?
insights.body: Solomon asks, "will God in very deed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens can't contain you; how much less this house" (8:27). The Temple is the place where God puts his name (8:29), not a box that holds him. Stephen and Paul later quote the same idea.

insights.title: Hear in heaven
insights.body: Seven times Solomon asks God to hear from heaven when people pray toward this house: after sin, in drought, famine, war, even in exile (8:30-50). The Temple becomes a direction of prayer. Daniel prays toward Jerusalem in Babylon.

insights.title: The foreigner too
insights.body: Solomon prays for the foreigner who comes "for your name's sake" (8:41-43), "that all the peoples of the earth may know your name." Isaiah calls the Temple "a house of prayer for all peoples," which Jesus quotes when he clears the Temple.

insights.title: No one who doesn't sin
insights.body: "There is no man who doesn't sin" (8:46), Solomon admits, and he foresees exile and asks God to forgive those who repent there. The prayer anticipates the very disaster that ends Kings.

insights.title: Feast of Tents
insights.body: The dedication takes place in the seventh month at the feast (8:2), the Feast of Tents, and lasts fourteen days (8:65). The vast number of sacrifices, twenty-two thousand cattle and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep (8:63), marks it as the greatest celebration of the age.

insights.title: A place to pray toward
insights.body: Israel prayed toward the Temple wherever they were. What helps you turn your heart toward God when you pray?

9.summary: God appears to Solomon a second time, promising to establish his throne if he obeys and warning of ruin if he turns away; Solomon gives Hiram twenty towns, uses forced labour, builds cities and a fleet.
9.lookfor: Notice the two sides of God's warning, Hiram's reaction to the towns, and who did the forced labour.

names.name: Cabul
names.gloss: A name Hiram gave the Galilean towns, perhaps meaning "as nothing."

names.name: Hazor
names.gloss: A major northern city rebuilt by Solomon.

names.name: Megiddo
names.gloss: A strategic city guarding the Jezreel valley.

names.name: Gezer
names.gloss: A city on the coastal route, given as a dowry with Pharaoh's daughter.

names.name: Ezion Geber
names.gloss: Solomon's port on the Gulf of Aqaba.

names.name: Ophir
names.gloss: A distant land famous for gold, of uncertain location.

insights.title: If and if not
insights.body: God promises a lasting throne "if you will walk before me, as David your father walked" (9:4-5), and warns that if Solomon or his sons turn to other gods, Israel will be cut off and the Temple become a heap of ruins (9:6-8). The rest of Kings shows the warning fulfilled.

insights.title: People will ask why
insights.body: Passers-by will hiss and ask, "Why has Yahweh done this to this land?" and be told it is because Israel forsook God (9:8-9). The same question and answer appear in Deuteronomy and Jeremiah.

insights.title: Towns that didn't please
insights.body: Solomon gives Hiram twenty towns in Galilee, but Hiram calls them "Cabul" (9:13), perhaps meaning "good for nothing." The great trade relationship had its tensions. Solomon also seems to owe Hiram gold (9:14).

insights.title: Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer
insights.body: Solomon fortifies Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer (9:15). Archaeologists found similar six-chambered gates at all three, which many dated to Solomon's time. The dating is now debated, but the three cities' strategic role is clear.

insights.title: Who were the labourers?
insights.body: Here the forced labourers are the remaining Canaanite peoples, while Israelites served as soldiers and officers (9:20-22). Chapter 5 says Israelites were drafted too. The two pictures may describe permanent slaves and temporary work gangs.

insights.title: Ships to Ophir
insights.body: Solomon builds a fleet at Ezion Geber on the Red Sea, crewed with Hiram's sailors, which brings gold from Ophir (9:26-28). Ophir's location is unknown; proposals include Arabia, East Africa and India. A pottery fragment found near Tel Aviv mentions "gold of Ophir."

insights.title: Conditions
insights.body: God's promise came with a warning. How do you hold together God's faithfulness and your responsibility to obey?

10.summary: The queen of Sheba visits to test Solomon's wisdom and is overwhelmed; the chapter describes Solomon's vast wealth in gold, his ivory throne, trade and horses.
10.lookfor: Notice why the queen came, what impresses her, and the growing lists of gold, horses and chariots.

names.name: Sheba
names.gloss: A kingdom probably in southwest Arabia, modern Yemen, rich from the incense trade.

names.name: Ophir
names.gloss: A distant source of gold.

names.name: Tarshish
names.gloss: A far-off port, probably in the western Mediterranean.

insights.title: The queen of Sheba
insights.body: Sheba was probably the kingdom of Saba in southwest Arabia, which grew rich from frankincense and myrrh caravans. Her visit may have had a trade purpose too. Ethiopian tradition holds that she bore Solomon a son, Menelik, founder of its royal line; the Bible says nothing of this.

insights.title: Not even half
insights.body: After seeing it all, the queen says, "not even half was told me!" (10:7), and blesses Yahweh who delighted in Solomon (10:9). She sees that the purpose of his kingship is "to do justice and righteousness."

insights.title: Something greater than Solomon
insights.body: Jesus says the queen of the south will rise in judgment against his generation, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon's wisdom, "and behold, someone greater than Solomon is here." A foreign queen travelled far to hear wisdom, and Jesus contrasts her eagerness with those who ignore the wisdom standing in front of them.

insights.title: 666 talents
insights.body: Solomon's yearly income in gold was "six hundred sixty-six talents" (10:14), over twenty tonnes. Some readers link the number with the beast's number in Revelation, though the connection is uncertain.

insights.title: Ivory throne
insights.body: Solomon's throne was ivory overlaid with gold, with six steps and twelve lions (10:18-20). Ivory furniture was a sign of royal luxury across the region; carved ivory panels have been found at Samaria and elsewhere.

insights.title: Horses from Egypt
insights.body: Solomon gathers chariots and horsemen and imports horses from Egypt (10:26-29), along with silver "as common as stones" (10:27). Deuteronomy forbade the king to multiply horses, return people to Egypt, or amass silver and gold. The glory carries the seeds of the fall.

insights.title: The nations come
insights.body: "All the earth sought the presence of Solomon, to hear his wisdom, which God had put in his heart" (10:24). The prophets picture nations streaming to Jerusalem in the age to come. Solomon's reign gives a glimpse of that hope.

insights.title: Glory and danger
insights.body: Solomon's success contained the seeds of his downfall. How can blessings become dangers?

11.summary: In old age Solomon's many foreign wives turn his heart to other gods; God announces that most of the kingdom will be torn from his son, raises up enemies, and the prophet Ahijah promises ten tribes to Jeroboam.
11.lookfor: Notice how Solomon's heart is described, why one tribe is left to David's line, and the torn cloak.

names.name: Ashtoreth
names.gloss: Astarte, a Phoenician goddess of fertility and war.

names.name: Milcom
names.gloss: The national god of the Ammonites, also called Molech.

names.name: Chemosh
names.gloss: The national god of Moab.

names.name: Hadad
names.gloss: An Edomite prince who became Solomon's enemy.

names.name: Rezon
names.gloss: A rebel who seized Damascus.

names.name: Jeroboam
names.gloss: An Ephraimite official over forced labour, promised ten tribes.

names.name: Ahijah
names.gloss: A prophet from Shiloh.

insights.title: Seven hundred wives
insights.body: Solomon had "seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines" (11:3). Many were political marriages to seal alliances. Deuteronomy had warned that many wives would turn a king's heart away.

insights.title: When Solomon was old
insights.body: "When Solomon was old, his wives turned away his heart after other gods" (11:4). The fall comes late, gradually, by accommodation. He built high places for Chemosh and Molech on the hill east of Jerusalem (11:7).

insights.title: Not perfect as David
insights.body: Solomon's heart "was not perfect with Yahweh his God, as the heart of David his father was" (11:4). David sinned grievously but never worshipped other gods. From here, every king will be measured against David.

insights.title: For David's sake
insights.body: God will tear the kingdom away, but not in Solomon's lifetime, and will leave one tribe "for David my servant's sake, and for Jerusalem's sake" (11:12-13). God's promise to David holds even when David's son fails.

insights.title: Enemies raised up
insights.body: God raises adversaries: Hadad of Edom and Rezon of Damascus (11:14, 11:23). The same Hebrew word, satan, adversary, is used for them. Peace on every side (5:4) gives way to opposition.

insights.title: A torn cloak
insights.body: Ahijah tears his new cloak into twelve pieces and tells Jeroboam to take ten (11:30-31). Prophets often acted out their messages. The torn garment recalls Samuel's robe torn when the kingdom was taken from Saul.

insights.title: A lamp in Jerusalem
insights.body: God promises that David will "have a lamp always before me in Jerusalem" (11:36). The lamp image returns as Judah survives kings who deserve to be cut off.

insights.title: A divided heart
insights.body: Solomon's fall was slow and late. What small accommodations could gradually pull your heart away from God?

12.summary: At Shechem Solomon's son Rehoboam refuses to lighten the people's burden, and the ten northern tribes break away under Jeroboam, who sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan to keep his people from Jerusalem.
12.lookfor: Notice the two pieces of advice Rehoboam receives, the northern cry, and the reasons Jeroboam gives for his calves.

names.name: Rehoboam
names.gloss: Solomon's son and heir.

names.name: Shechem
names.gloss: An ancient city in the northern hill country, where Joshua renewed the covenant.

names.name: Jeroboam
names.gloss: The Ephraimite who becomes the first king of the northern kingdom.

names.name: Adoram
names.gloss: Officer over forced labour, stoned by the northern tribes.

names.name: Shemaiah
names.gloss: A prophet who forbids civil war.

names.name: Bethel
names.gloss: An ancient sanctuary on the southern edge of the northern kingdom.

names.name: Dan
names.gloss: A town in the far north, near the springs of the Jordan.

insights.title: Lighten the yoke
insights.body: The people ask, "make the hard service of your father, and his heavy yoke which he put on us, lighter" (12:4). Solomon's building and labour drafts had cost them dearly. Rehoboam is offered a chance to reign by serving.

insights.title: A servant to this people
insights.body: The old advisers say, "If you will be a servant to this people today... then they will be your servants forever" (12:7). Rehoboam rejects this for the young men's boast: "My little finger is thicker than my father's waist" (12:10). Jesus later teaches that the greatest must be the servant.

insights.title: Whips and scorpions
insights.body: "My father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions" (12:14). Scorpions may mean whips with metal barbs. The harsh words cost Rehoboam ten tribes.

insights.title: To your tents, Israel
insights.body: The north answers, "What portion have we in David?... To your tents, Israel!" (12:16). Sheba had raised the same cry against David. The old north–south rift opens for good.

insights.title: This thing is from me
insights.body: God tells Rehoboam not to fight, "for this thing is from me" (12:24). The split fulfils Ahijah's word. Human pride and God's judgment work together in the same event.

insights.title: Golden calves
insights.body: Jeroboam makes two golden calves and says, "behold your gods, Israel, which brought you up out of the land of Egypt!" (12:28), almost the words of Aaron at Sinai. He may have meant the calves as pedestals for an invisible Yahweh, but Kings treats them as idolatry. "The sins of Jeroboam" becomes the refrain for every northern king.

insights.title: Bethel and Dan
insights.body: Jeroboam places the calves at Bethel in the south and Dan in the north (12:29), both old sanctuaries. At Tel Dan archaeologists found a large cult platform from the period of the divided kingdom. Jeroboam also appoints non-Levite priests and moves a festival to the eighth month (12:31-33).

insights.title: Servant or master
insights.body: Rehoboam chose to rule by force rather than by serving. In your influence over others, which do you lean toward?

13.summary: A man of God from Judah denounces Jeroboam's altar at Bethel and foretells King Josiah, but on his way home he is deceived by an old prophet into disobeying God's command and is killed by a lion.
13.lookfor: Notice the signs at the altar, the old prophet's lie, and the strange scene of the lion and the donkey.

names.name: Josiah
names.gloss: A king of Judah who would reign about three hundred years later.

names.name: Bethel
names.gloss: The site of one of Jeroboam's golden calves.

insights.title: Josiah by name
insights.body: The man of God cries, "a son will be born to David's house, Josiah by name" (13:2), who will burn priests' bones on this altar. Three centuries later Josiah does exactly this. Some scholars think the name was added after the event; the text presents it as prophecy.

insights.title: A withered hand
insights.body: Jeroboam points at the prophet to have him seized, and his hand dries up (13:4). The altar splits and its ashes pour out (13:5). Jeroboam begs for prayer, and his hand is restored (13:6).

insights.title: Don't eat or drink there
insights.body: God had told the man of God not to eat or drink in Bethel or return the same way (13:9). Refusing hospitality marked the northern sanctuary as under judgment. His obedience is the message.

insights.title: He lied to him
insights.body: An old prophet claims an angel told him to bring the man home, and the narrator adds bluntly, "He lied to him" (13:18). The man of God trusts a fellow prophet's claim over God's direct word.

insights.title: A lion that didn't eat
insights.body: A lion kills the man of God but stands beside the body without eating it or the donkey (13:24-28). Lions lived in Israel then. The unnatural scene marks the death as God's judgment, not chance.

insights.title: Buried together
insights.body: The old prophet buries the man of God in his own tomb, mourns him, and asks to be buried beside him (13:30-31). When Josiah later digs up the bones at Bethel, he leaves these two graves alone.

insights.title: Jeroboam didn't turn
insights.body: "After this thing Jeroboam didn't return from his evil way" (13:33). Even with miracles before his eyes, he goes on appointing priests for the high places. This becomes the sin that destroys his house.

insights.title: Testing claims
insights.body: The man of God believed someone who claimed a message from God. How do you test claims to speak for God?

14.summary: Jeroboam's wife visits the blind prophet Ahijah in disguise and hears judgment on Jeroboam's house; their son dies; in Judah, Rehoboam's people turn to idolatry and Pharaoh Shishak plunders Jerusalem.
14.lookfor: Notice the failed disguise, what Ahijah says about the dying child, and what Shishak takes.

names.name: Ahijah
names.gloss: The prophet of Shiloh who had promised Jeroboam the kingdom.

names.name: Abijah
names.gloss: Jeroboam's son, who falls ill.

names.name: Tirzah
names.gloss: A city that served as an early capital of the northern kingdom.

names.name: Shishak
names.gloss: Pharaoh of Egypt, known from Egyptian records as Sheshonq I.

names.name: Naamah
names.gloss: Rehoboam's mother, an Ammonite.

insights.title: A blind prophet sees
insights.body: Jeroboam's wife disguises herself, but the old blind prophet knows her before she enters (14:4-6). God had told him. No disguise works before God.

insights.title: Cast me behind your back
insights.body: Ahijah's verdict: Jeroboam has "cast me behind your back" (14:9). The man God raised up has done worse than all before him. His house will be swept away like dung (14:10).

insights.title: Some good thing
insights.body: Only the sick boy will be buried with honour, "because in him there is found some good thing toward Yahweh" (14:13). The child's death is a mercy in a doomed house. It is a hard and tender verse.

insights.title: Beyond the River
insights.body: Ahijah foresees Israel uprooted and scattered "beyond the River" (14:15), the Euphrates. Two centuries later Assyria deports the northern kingdom.

insights.title: Shishak's campaign
insights.body: In Rehoboam's fifth year, Shishak king of Egypt takes the Temple and palace treasures, including Solomon's gold shields (14:25-26). Egyptian records confirm a campaign by Sheshonq I into Canaan around 925 BC, listing many towns on a temple wall at Karnak.

insights.title: Bronze for gold
insights.body: Rehoboam replaces the gold shields with bronze ones (14:27), kept in the guardroom and carried out when the king went to the Temple. The glitter of Solomon's age is gone, replaced by imitation.

insights.title: Judah no better
insights.body: Judah builds high places, pillars and Asherah poles "on every high hill, and under every green tree" (14:23), with shrine prostitutes in the land (14:24). The south is not innocent; both kingdoms drift.

insights.title: Some good thing
insights.body: God noticed some good in one child in a corrupt family. What does that suggest about how God sees individuals?

15.summary: Abijam and then Asa reign in Judah, with Asa removing idols and his own mother's Asherah image; in Israel, Nadab son of Jeroboam is killed by Baasha, who wipes out Jeroboam's house.
15.lookfor: Notice the formula used for each king, how Asa is judged, and how Ahijah's prophecy is fulfilled.

names.name: Abijam
names.gloss: Rehoboam's son, king of Judah for three years.

names.name: Asa
names.gloss: Abijam's son, a reforming king of Judah who reigned forty-one years.

names.name: Maacah
names.gloss: Asa's grandmother, the queen mother, who made an idol.

names.name: Ben Hadad
names.gloss: King of Aram in Damascus.

names.name: Nadab
names.gloss: Jeroboam's son, king of Israel for two years.

names.name: Baasha
names.gloss: The man who killed Nadab and became king of Israel.

skim.advice: Much of the chapter uses the standard formulas for each king's reign. Skim them, and read the verdicts on Abijam and Asa (verses 3 to 5 and 11 to 14) and the fulfilment in verses 29 to 30 closely.

insights.title: The regnal formula
insights.body: Each king is introduced with the year he began in relation to the other kingdom's king, his age, the length of his reign, his mother's name for Judah, and a verdict (15:1-3, 15:9-11). The book refers readers to royal annals, now lost, for more (15:7).

insights.title: Except Uriah
insights.body: David "didn't turn away from anything that he commanded him all the days of his life, except only in the matter of Uriah the Hittite" (15:5). Even in praising David, the narrator does not forget his great sin.

insights.title: A lamp for David
insights.body: Abijam's heart was not perfect, "Nevertheless for David's sake" God kept "a lamp in Jerusalem" (15:4). The dynasty survives bad kings because of God's promise.

insights.title: Removing the queen mother
insights.body: Asa removes his grandmother Maacah from being queen mother because she made "an abominable image for an Asherah" and burns it at the Kidron (15:13). The queen mother had real power in Judah; Asa puts God before family.

insights.title: But the high places
insights.body: "But the high places were not taken away. Nevertheless the heart of Asa was perfect with Yahweh" (15:14). The phrase "the high places were not taken away" recurs for good kings until Hezekiah. Reform is real but incomplete.

insights.title: Buying Aram's help
insights.body: Asa sends the Temple's silver and gold to Ben Hadad of Damascus to break his treaty with Israel (15:18-19). It works, but Chronicles records a prophet rebuking Asa for relying on Aram instead of God.

insights.title: Jeroboam's house wiped out
insights.body: Baasha kills Nadab and strikes "all the house of Jeroboam" (15:29), as Ahijah had prophesied. Israel's kings will fall by assassination again and again. Judah's dynasty, by contrast, lasts.

insights.title: Incomplete reform
insights.body: Asa's heart was right, but the high places remained. What areas of your life have you never fully surrendered?

16.summary: A rapid series of northern kings: Baasha's house is destroyed by Zimri, who reigns seven days before Omri takes power, builds Samaria, and is succeeded by Ahab, who marries Jezebel and serves Baal.
16.lookfor: Notice how quickly kings fall, the founding of Samaria, and how Ahab is introduced.

names.name: Jehu
names.gloss: A prophet, son of Hanani (not the later king Jehu).

names.name: Elah
names.gloss: Baasha's son, killed while drunk.

names.name: Zimri
names.gloss: A chariot commander who reigned seven days.

names.name: Omri
names.gloss: Army commander who founded a powerful dynasty.

names.name: Samaria
names.gloss: The new northern capital Omri built on a hill.

names.name: Ahab
names.gloss: Omri's son, the most notorious king of Israel.

names.name: Jezebel
names.gloss: A Phoenician princess, daughter of the king of Sidon, Ahab's wife.

names.name: Hiel
names.gloss: A man of Bethel who rebuilt Jericho.

skim.advice: Verses 1 to 22 move rapidly through short reigns using standard formulas. Skim them, and read the accounts of Omri and Ahab (verses 23 to 34) closely.

insights.title: Seven-day king
insights.body: Zimri kills Elah while he is drunk and reigns seven days in Tirzah (16:9-15). When the army makes Omri king, Zimri burns the palace over himself (16:18). His name became a byword for a traitor.

insights.title: Omri the great
insights.body: Kings gives Omri only a few verses, yet he was a major ruler. The Moabite Mesha Stele says Omri oppressed Moab for many years, and Assyrian records called Israel "the house of Omri" long after his dynasty ended.

insights.title: Building Samaria
insights.body: Omri buys the hill of Samaria for two talents of silver (16:24) and builds a new capital. Excavations show fine royal buildings and carved ivories from the following decades. Samaria gave its name to the whole region.

insights.title: Worse than all before
insights.body: Omri "dealt wickedly above all who were before him" (16:25), and Ahab did evil "above all that were before him" (16:30). Kings judges kings by faithfulness to Yahweh, not by political success.

insights.title: Jezebel and Baal
insights.body: As if Jeroboam's sins were "a light thing," Ahab marries Jezebel daughter of Ethbaal of Sidon and serves Baal, building him a temple in Samaria (16:31-32). Baal was a Canaanite storm god believed to send rain. The stage is set for Elijah.

insights.title: Jericho rebuilt
insights.body: Hiel of Bethel rebuilds Jericho at the cost of his firstborn and youngest sons (16:34), fulfilling Joshua's curse. The note shows God's word still standing, centuries later, in an age that ignores it.

insights.title: Civil war
insights.body: Israel splits between Omri and Tibni for some years before Omri prevails (16:21-22). The north has no settled dynasty; power belongs to whoever controls the army.

insights.title: Success and faithfulness
insights.body: Omri was powerful, yet the Bible gives him a few lines and a bad verdict. How does God's measure of a life differ from the world's?

17.summary: Elijah announces a drought to Ahab, is fed by ravens at a brook, then by a widow in Zarephath whose flour and oil never run out, and raises her son from the dead.
17.lookfor: Notice who provides for Elijah, where the widow lives, and what she says at the end.

names.name: Elijah
names.gloss: A prophet from Tishbe in Gilead; his name means "Yahweh is my God."

names.name: Gilead
names.gloss: The hilly region east of the Jordan.

names.name: Cherith
names.gloss: A brook east of the Jordan where Elijah hid.

names.name: Zarephath
names.gloss: A Phoenician town between Tyre and Sidon, Jezebel's home territory.

insights.title: No dew nor rain
insights.body: Elijah tells Ahab there will be no dew or rain "but according to my word" (17:1). Baal was the storm god who supposedly sent rain. The drought is a direct challenge: who really controls the rain?

insights.title: Fed by ravens
insights.body: At the brook Cherith ravens bring Elijah bread and meat morning and evening (17:6). Ravens were unclean birds. God provides through unlikely means.

insights.title: A widow of Sidon
insights.body: God sends Elijah to a widow in Zarephath, in Sidon, Jezebel's homeland (17:9). Jesus points to this in Nazareth: there were many widows in Israel, but Elijah was sent to a foreign one.

insights.title: The last meal
insights.body: The widow is gathering sticks to bake her last flour and oil "that we may eat it, and die" (17:12). Elijah asks for a cake first. "The jar of meal didn't run out, and the jar of oil did not fail" (17:16).

insights.title: The son raised
insights.body: When her son dies, the widow blames Elijah (17:18). He carries the boy upstairs, stretches himself on him three times and prays, and the child lives (17:21-22). It is the first resurrection recorded in the Bible.

insights.title: Now I know
insights.body: The widow says, "Now I know that you are a man of God, and that Yahweh's word in your mouth is truth" (17:24). A foreign woman confesses what Israel's king refuses to see.

insights.title: Elijah's name
insights.body: Elijah's name means "Yahweh is my God," a summary of his whole mission against Baal. On Mount Carmel the people will cry out almost his name: "Yahweh, he is God!"

insights.title: Giving first
insights.body: The widow fed the prophet from her last flour. When has trusting God meant giving before you could see how you'd be provided for?

18.summary: In the third year of drought Elijah confronts Ahab and challenges the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel; Baal does not answer, God sends fire on Elijah's soaked altar, the people confess Yahweh, the prophets are killed, and rain comes.
18.lookfor: Notice Obadiah's divided position, Elijah's challenge to the people, his mockery, and the small cloud.

names.name: Obadiah
names.gloss: Ahab's palace manager, who secretly hid a hundred prophets.

names.name: Mount Carmel
names.gloss: A mountain ridge by the Mediterranean in northern Israel.

names.name: Kishon
names.gloss: A brook below Mount Carmel.

names.name: Jezreel
names.gloss: Ahab's second royal city, in the Jezreel valley.

insights.title: Obadiah in the palace
insights.body: Obadiah "feared Yahweh greatly" (18:3) and hid a hundred prophets from Jezebel in caves (18:4), yet served Ahab. He is terrified to report Elijah. He shows a believer working faithfully inside a hostile regime.

insights.title: Troubler of Israel
insights.body: Ahab greets Elijah: "Is that you, you troubler of Israel?" (18:17). Elijah replies that Ahab is the troubler, for forsaking God (18:18). The word was used of Achan, whose sin brought disaster on Israel.

insights.title: Limping between two opinions
insights.body: "How long will you waver between the two sides? If Yahweh is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him" (18:21). The verb pictures limping or hopping. The people's silence shows their divided hearts.

insights.title: Is Baal asleep?
insights.body: Elijah mocks: perhaps Baal "is deep in thought, or he has gone somewhere, or he is on a journey, or perhaps he sleeps" (18:27). Canaanite texts from Ugarit describe Baal dying and reviving, travelling and feasting. The prophets cut themselves, a known ritual (18:28), but there was "no voice, no answer, and nobody paid attention" (18:29).

insights.title: Twelve stones and water
insights.body: Elijah rebuilds Yahweh's altar with twelve stones for the tribes (18:31) and drenches it with twelve jars of water (18:33-35). In a drought, the water is costly. Then "Yahweh's fire fell" and consumed even the stones and water (18:38).

insights.title: Yahweh, he is God
insights.body: The people fall on their faces: "Yahweh, he is God! Yahweh, he is God!" (18:39). It echoes Moses' teaching and Elijah's own name. Then Elijah has the prophets of Baal killed at the Kishon (18:40), following the Law's penalty for false prophets, a grim end to the contest.

insights.title: A cloud like a hand
insights.body: Elijah prays with his face between his knees and sends his servant seven times to look at the sea; the seventh time, "a small cloud, like a man's hand" (18:44). James cites Elijah as an example of persistent prayer.

insights.title: Two opinions
insights.body: Israel tried to keep both Yahweh and Baal. What divided loyalties are you living with?

19.summary: Threatened by Jezebel, Elijah flees to the wilderness and asks to die; an angel feeds him, he journeys to Horeb, meets God in a gentle whisper rather than wind, earthquake or fire, and is sent to anoint kings and Elisha.
19.lookfor: Notice Elijah's despair after victory, how God cares for him, the question God asks twice, and where God is not found.

names.name: Jezebel
names.gloss: Ahab's queen, devoted to Baal.

names.name: Beersheba
names.gloss: A town at the southern edge of Judah.

names.name: Horeb
names.gloss: Mount Sinai, where God spoke to Moses.

names.name: Hazael
names.gloss: A future king of Aram (Syria).

names.name: Jehu
names.gloss: A future king of Israel who would destroy Ahab's house.

names.name: Elisha
names.gloss: A farmer's son who becomes Elijah's successor.

insights.title: After the mountaintop
insights.body: Right after Carmel, one threat from Jezebel sends Elijah running (19:2-3). He sits under a broom tree and asks to die: "It is enough" (19:4). Spiritual highs can be followed by deep lows.

insights.title: Sleep and food
insights.body: God's first answer to Elijah's despair is not a rebuke but bread, water and sleep, twice (19:5-8). "The journey is too great for you" (19:7). Care for the body comes before words.

insights.title: Forty days to Horeb
insights.body: Strengthened by the food, Elijah travels forty days and nights to Horeb (19:8). Moses spent forty days on the same mountain, and Jesus fasted forty days in the wilderness. Elijah goes back to where Israel's covenant began.

insights.title: What are you doing here?
insights.body: Twice God asks, "What are you doing here, Elijah?" (19:9, 19:13). Twice Elijah gives the same answer: he alone is left (19:10, 19:14). God lets him say it, then gives him new work.

insights.title: A still small voice
insights.body: God was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in "a still small voice" (19:12). The Hebrew is something like a sound of thin silence. At Sinai God had come in fire and thunder; here he comes quietly.

insights.title: Seven thousand
insights.body: Elijah thinks he alone is faithful, but God has kept "seven thousand in Israel, all the knees of which have not bowed to Baal" (19:18). Paul quotes this to show God always keeps a remnant by grace.

insights.title: The mantle
insights.body: Elijah finds Elisha ploughing with twelve yoke of oxen and throws his cloak over him (19:19). The mantle signals a claim and a calling. Elisha slaughters his oxen and burns the yoke to cook them (19:21), leaving his old life behind.

insights.title: I alone am left
insights.body: Elijah felt completely alone. When have you felt that way, and how did God show you otherwise?

20.summary: Ben Hadad of Aram besieges Samaria with thirty-two kings; a prophet promises victory, Israel wins twice, but Ahab spares Ben Hadad and makes a treaty, and a prophet condemns him for it.
20.lookfor: Notice Ben Hadad's arrogance, Ahab's proverb, the Arameans' theory about Israel's God, and the prophet's acted parable.

names.name: Ben Hadad
names.gloss: King of Aram, based in Damascus.

names.name: Aphek
names.gloss: A town east of the Sea of Galilee where the second battle was fought.

insights.title: Don't boast too soon
insights.body: To Ben Hadad's threats Ahab replies, "Don't let him who puts on his armor brag like he who takes it off" (20:11). It is a proverb of the time, and a wise one, even from Ahab.

insights.title: Drunk in the booths
insights.body: Ben Hadad and the thirty-two kings are drinking in their booths when Israel attacks at noon (20:16). Arrogance and drink cost them the battle.

insights.title: God of the hills
insights.body: The Arameans think Israel's god is "a god of the hills" and plan to fight in the plain (20:23). God answers through a prophet: because they said this, "I will deliver all this great multitude into your hand" (20:28). Yahweh is not a local god.

insights.title: Sackcloth and ropes
insights.body: Defeated, Ben Hadad's servants come with sackcloth on their loins and ropes on their heads to beg for mercy (20:31-32). Ahab calls him "my brother" and makes a treaty (20:33-34).

insights.title: Devoted to destruction
insights.body: A prophet, disguised as a wounded soldier, tells a story that makes Ahab condemn himself (20:39-40), like Nathan with David. Because Ahab let go the man God had "devoted to destruction," his life will pay (20:42).

insights.title: Sullen and angry
insights.body: Ahab goes home "sullen and angry" (20:43). The same words describe him in the next chapter when Naboth refuses him. Rebuke makes him sulk, not repent.

insights.title: Markets in Damascus
insights.body: Ben Hadad offers Ahab trading streets in Damascus (20:34), like those his father had in Samaria. Commercial quarters for foreign merchants were a common part of ancient treaties.

insights.title: Mercy in the wrong place
insights.body: Ahab was generous to an enemy king and ruthless to his own subject Naboth. How can misplaced mercy and misplaced harshness both be wrong?

21.summary: Naboth refuses to sell Ahab his family vineyard; Jezebel arranges false charges and his stoning, and Ahab takes the vineyard, but Elijah pronounces doom on Ahab and Jezebel, and Ahab humbles himself.
21.lookfor: Notice why Naboth refuses, how Jezebel uses legal forms to murder, and God's response to Ahab's repentance.

names.name: Naboth
names.gloss: A man of Jezreel whose vineyard lay next to Ahab's palace.

names.name: Jezebel
names.gloss: Ahab's queen, from Sidon.

names.name: Elijah the Tishbite
names.gloss: The prophet who confronts Ahab.

insights.title: The inheritance of my fathers
insights.body: Naboth refuses: "May Yahweh forbid me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers to you!" (21:3). Family land was a trust from God, not merchandise. The Law protected such inheritances.

insights.title: A sulking king
insights.body: Ahab goes home "sullen and angry," lies on his bed, turns his face away and won't eat (21:4). The most powerful man in Israel acts like a spoiled child.

insights.title: Do you now govern?
insights.body: Jezebel asks, "Do you now govern the kingdom of Israel?" (21:7). In her Phoenician world, kings took what they wanted. Israel's law limited the king, and Jezebel shows her contempt for it.

insights.title: Murder by legal process
insights.body: Jezebel writes letters in Ahab's name, proclaims a fast, and has two worthless men accuse Naboth of cursing God and the king (21:9-10). He is stoned, and his sons too (2 Kings 9:26). She uses the Law's form, two witnesses, to break its heart.

insights.title: Killed and taken possession
insights.body: Elijah meets Ahab in the vineyard: "Have you killed and also taken possession?" (21:19), and "dogs will lick your blood" (21:19). Ahab says, "Have you found me, my enemy?" (21:20). Like David with Uriah, a king has killed to take what he wanted.

insights.title: Sold himself
insights.body: "There was no one like Ahab, who sold himself to do that which was evil in Yahweh's sight, whom Jezebel his wife stirred up" (21:25). The verdict is severe, and it notes Jezebel's influence.

insights.title: Ahab humbles himself
insights.body: Ahab tears his clothes, wears sackcloth and fasts (21:27). God tells Elijah, "See how Ahab humbles himself before me?" and delays the disaster to his son's days (21:29). Even Ahab's repentance is noticed.

insights.title: Abuse of power
insights.body: Naboth's story is about the powerful taking from the weak under cover of law. Where do you see that happening today, and what is your response?

22.summary: Ahab and Jehoshaphat of Judah plan to retake Ramoth Gilead; four hundred prophets promise victory, but Micaiah foresees defeat; Ahab disguises himself, yet a random arrow kills him; Jehoshaphat's and Ahaziah's reigns are summarised.
22.lookfor: Notice why Jehoshaphat asks for another prophet, Micaiah's vision, the disguise, and how Elijah's word comes true.

names.name: Jehoshaphat
names.gloss: King of Judah, son of Asa, allied with Ahab.

names.name: Ramoth Gilead
names.gloss: A city east of the Jordan disputed between Israel and Aram.

names.name: Micaiah
names.gloss: A prophet, son of Imlah, who speaks only what God says.

names.name: Zedekiah
names.gloss: One of Ahab's court prophets.

names.name: Ahaziah
names.gloss: Ahab's son and successor.

insights.title: One more prophet
insights.body: Four hundred prophets say go, but Jehoshaphat asks, "Isn't there here a prophet of Yahweh, that we may inquire of him?" (22:7). Ahab admits there is one, "but I hate him, for he does not prophesy good concerning me" (22:8).

insights.title: Iron horns
insights.body: Zedekiah makes iron horns and declares Ahab will gore the Arameans (22:11). Prophets often acted out their messages. The horn was a symbol of strength.

insights.title: Sheep without a shepherd
insights.body: Micaiah sees "all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd" (22:17), a picture of Ahab's death. Moses had prayed that Israel would never be like that, and Jesus had compassion on crowds who were.

insights.title: A lying spirit
insights.body: Micaiah describes a vision of God's council, where a spirit offers to be "a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets" (22:22). It is one of the Bible's most puzzling scenes. Interpreters see God giving Ahab over to the falsehood he preferred, while still sending Micaiah to tell him the truth.

insights.title: Faithful at a cost
insights.body: Micaiah vows, "what Yahweh says to me, that I will speak" (22:14). He is slapped and imprisoned on bread and water (22:24-27). His last words: "If you return at all in peace, Yahweh has not spoken by me" (22:28).

insights.title: An arrow at random
insights.body: Ahab disguises himself, but "a certain man drew his bow at random" and hits him between the joints of his armour (22:34). No disguise can hide him from God's word. He bleeds to death propped up in his chariot (22:35).

insights.title: Dogs licked his blood
insights.body: His chariot is washed at the pool of Samaria, and the dogs lick his blood (22:38), as Elijah had foretold. The detail about prostitutes bathing there adds to the shame.

insights.title: Wanting to hear good news
insights.body: Ahab gathered prophets who told him what he wanted. Do you seek out voices that will tell you the truth, even when it is unwelcome?

intro.who: The author is not named; the Talmud credits Jeremiah. Many modern scholars see 1 and 2 Kings as the last part of a history running from Deuteronomy to Kings, compiled from royal annals and prophetic stories and finished during the Babylonian exile.
intro.when: 1 Kings runs from David's death and Solomon's accession, around 970 BC, to the death of Ahab and the reign of his son Ahaziah, around 850 BC. 1 and 2 Kings were one book in Hebrew; the Greek translation called them 3 and 4 Kingdoms.
intro.why: It tells how Solomon's glorious kingdom, with its Temple, split in two after his unfaithfulness, and how kings in both kingdoms are judged by one question: did they worship Yahweh alone? The prophets, above all Elijah, confront kings who turn to Baal.
